title: Machine learning of systemic metabolic profiles and longitudinal trajectories for risk stratification in HBV-related chronic liver disease
abstract: Existing clinical indices, such as the albumin–bilirubin (ALBI) score and fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) index, serve as pragmatic bedside benchmarks but face limitations in capturing the dynamic nature of hepatic decompensation. This study aimed to investigate whether integrating broad systemic metabolic profiles with early longitudinal ALBI trajectories can refine risk stratification within a large-scale, heterogeneous hepatitis B virus (HBV)-related chronic liver disease cohort. We conducted a retrospective cohort study tracking 11,768 patients with HBV-related conditions (including inactive carriers, chronic hepatitis B, compensated cirrhosis, and decompensated cirrhosis). The cohort was partitioned into a training/validation set ( n = 8,267) and an independent test set ( n = 3,501). Machine learning frameworks (LASSO–Cox regression) were employed to construct a metabolic risk score. Trajectory clustering characterized ALBI measurements available by day 180, and a strict landmark sensitivity analysis assessed the feasibility of subsequent outcome comparisons. The random forest model showed high discrimination for severe ALBI grade classification (AUC 0.986), while the prognostic nomogram for event-free survival achieved time-dependent AUCs of 72.4%, 77.9%, and 82.1% at 3, 6, and 12 months. SHAP analysis indicated that systemic metabolic markers, especially the albumin-to-globulin (A/G) ratio, prealbumin, calcium, and magnesium, contributed strongly to ALBI severity classification. After restricting month 6 measurements to days 150–180, 96 patients had complete trajectories and 36 entered the landmark analysis. No subsequent events were recorded using the existing diagnosis-text endpoint, precluding between-group survival comparisons. Broad systemic metabolic profiling may contribute to risk stratification, although incremental prognostic value beyond conventional static scores remains to be established. Longitudinal ALBI trajectories describe heterogeneous biochemical patterns; their prognostic value could not be established because the strict day 180 landmark analysis had no subsequent recorded events.

title: Seroprevalence and risk of transmission of HBV, HCV and HIV in approved blood donors in southern Mozambique
abstract: Blood transfusion is an essential component of modern medical care. However, its use is associated with risks, including the transmission of infectious agents such as Hepatitis B Virus (HBV), Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) and Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV). Monitoring seroprevalence among approved blood donors is important for assessing transfusion safety. This study aimed to determine the seroprevalence and risk of transmission of HBV, HCV, and HIV among approved blood donors in Gaza and Inhambane provinces. A cross-sectional observational study was conducted among approved blood donors in eight health facilities in Gaza and Inhambane provinces between December 2022 and February 2024. Sociodemographic data and results from HBV, HCV, HIV serological testing were collected using the ODK Collect tool. Additional testing was conducted on plasma samples that were negative or indeterminate for the three pathogens using the cobas MPX. A total of 3,662 approved blood donors were included. Most participants were male (79.2%), aged 18–29 years (57.6%), and replacement donors (71.9%). The seroprevalence of HBV, HCV, and HIV was 1.3% (44; 95% CI: 0.9–1.7), 0.0% (0; 95% CI: 0.0–0.1), and 1.3% (46; 95% CI: 0.9–1.7), respectively. The frequency of HBV, HCV, and HIV positivity among samples that tested negative in serological tests was 18.7 (46; 95% CI: 13.7–24.9), 1.2 (3; 95 IC: 0.2–3.5) and 5.5 (14; 95 IC: 3.0–9.3) per 1000 blood units, respectively. The frequency of undetermined samples for HBV, HCV and HIV was 3.3% (119; 95% CI: 2.7–3.9), 2.4% (86; 95% CI: 1.9–2.9) and 0.2% (7; 95% CI: 0.08–0.40), respectively. The seroprevalence of HBV, HCV and HIV was low, however, a high risk of transfusion-transmitted infections was observed for all three pathogens. The study highlights the need to invest in testing and to strengthen the recruitment and retention of regular volunteer donors.
